title: Whose minutes?
hook: Three undertakings, nine trains, forecasts that may be off. Every minute you give one train, another pays.
text: 08:00 to 08:40 at the dispatcher's desk above the signal box of Bf Neustadt, on the lab's table. The signaller (the computer's seat) sets the routes; you say who waits for whom and how long, and which track a train takes. The regional trains, the intercity and the freight trains belong to three undertakings. Three trains come late, and how late is a forecast that may be off by minutes. Hold a train for a late feeder, and everybody aboard pays; let it go, and the changers wait half an hour. Let the freight train out before the late intercity, and the intercity may crawl behind it to the next loop; make it wait, and it stands on a track the next train needs. Each undertaking counts the minutes you add to its trains: its goodwill falls, it phones, and below a mark it writes to the regulator, whose verdict depends on whether you kept the rules of the line. No order suits all three. What you practise: the dispatching rules (a train on time before a late one, three minutes of waiting time), what an overtaking and a kept connection cost, reading a track occupation chart, deciding on a forecast, and staying fair between undertakings.

who.name: R. Dohle
who.role: Senior dispatcher, at the next desk

story.say: Morning. Today the desk above the signal box is yours: nine trains of three undertakings. You set no routes. You say who waits for whom, and how long. The signaller does the rest.

who.name: R. Dohle
who.role: Senior dispatcher, at the next desk

story.say: The window shows the three platform tracks over the morning: thin lines are the plan, thick ones what we expect now. Red: two trains want one track. Tap a train, on the table or in the window, to give it an order.

who.name: R. Dohle
who.role: Senior dispatcher, at the next desk

story.say: Mind the three numbers at the top: the goodwill of each undertaking. Every minute you add to a train costs its owner's. Below 62 they phone. Below 28 they write to the regulator.

who.name: R. Dohle
who.role: Senior dispatcher, at the next desk

story.say: The rule of the line: a train on time goes before a late one, and nobody is made to wait more than 3 min for another. Inside the rule you are covered. Whether it was wise is another matter.

who.name: R. Dohle
who.role: Senior dispatcher, at the next desk

story.say: A forecast is a guess from the next station. Once the train is really on its way you get the true figure: look at your orders again then. You can change one as long as its train stands.

who.name: R. Dohle
who.role: Senior dispatcher, at the next desk

story.say: A track can be changed only before a train comes: the signaller sets its route a minute ahead. G1 is the through track. What runs there crosses nobody at the island platform.

who.name: R. Dohle
who.role: Senior dispatcher, at the next desk

story.say: One more late feeder to come. By now you know whom you have asked to pay this morning. Spread it: an order that suits two of three is not good enough.

who.name: R. Dohle
who.role: Senior dispatcher, at the next desk

story.say: {train} comes {min} min late, not {told}. Does your order still fit? Tap the train and change it: a wait can be cut short or made longer while the train stands.

who.name: R. Dohle
who.role: Senior dispatcher, at the next desk

story.say: {train} waited {min} min and left without the passengers of {feeder}. A wait that is too short costs twice: the minutes and the connection. Long enough, or not at all.

who.name: R. Dohle
who.role: Senior dispatcher, at the next desk

story.say: {train} is crawling behind {slow} as far as the next loop: {min} min more. Letting the slow one out first is free only when the fast one is far behind.

who.name: R. Dohle
who.role: Senior dispatcher, at the next desk

story.say: {who} has written to the regulator, and the complaint is {verdict}. It holds when an on-time train of theirs waited beyond the rule for somebody else's late one.

who.name: R. Dohle
who.role: Senior dispatcher, at the next desk

story.say: You promised {who} a clear run for {train}, and it did not get one. Promise only what your own orders can keep. The rest is weather.

who.name: R. Dohle
who.role: Senior dispatcher, at the next desk

story.say: {train} is put aside: its driver's time ran out while it stood. Two minutes here have become an hour for the freight customer, and a track at the next station is blocked.

debrief: Whose minutes did your orders move this morning: from which train to which, from which undertaking to which? Would the three undertakings tell it the same way?
Where did a forecast turn out wrong? What would you have ordered had you known, and what does that say about waiting until you are sure?
Where did you leave the rule of the line (a train on time before a late one, three minutes of waiting), and could you defend that to the regulator?
What did you promise on the phone, and which other train paid for keeping it, or for breaking it?
